title: AI Explainability Tools
shortDefinition: Tools like SHAP and LIME that explain individual AI model predictions — which features drove this specific output?
definition: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) are the two most widely used tools for explaining individual AI model predictions — answering 'why did this model predict X for this specific input?' rather than just 'what does the model predict overall?' Both produce feature importance scores for individual predictions rather than global averages, enabling explanation of consequential individual decisions in a way that global feature importance statistics can't provide.

sections.title: SHAP: Game-theory-based attribution
sections.description: SHAP assigns each feature a contribution to the prediction using cooperative game theory — mathematically rigorous and theoretically defensible.

content.text: SHAP uses concepts from cooperative game theory to assign each feature a contribution to the model's prediction for a specific input — how much did each feature push the prediction up or down from the average? SHAP values have a mathematically rigorous property: they're the only attribution method satisfying certain fairness axioms (efficiency, symmetry, dummy, and additivity), making SHAP outputs more theoretically defensible than simpler attribution approaches. SHAP is computationally efficient for tree-based models (where exact SHAP values can be computed quickly) and approximated for other model types.

items: Game-theory based — cooperative game theory attribution.
Fairness axioms — efficiency, symmetry, dummy, additivity.
Theoretically defensible — rigorous mathematical foundation.
Tree efficient — exact values for tree-based models.
Approximated — for neural networks and other model types.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: SHAP provides mathematically rigorous feature attribution — the only method satisfying certain fairness axioms for individual prediction explanations.

sections.title: LIME: Local approximation explanation
sections.description: LIME explains predictions by fitting a simple interpretable model to the local neighborhood of a specific input — model-agnostic and widely applicable.

content.text: LIME explains a specific prediction by perturbing the input and fitting a simple, interpretable model (typically linear) to the model's behavior in the local neighborhood of that specific input — the simple local model's feature weights provide an explanation that's accurate near the prediction being explained, even if the global model is highly complex. LIME is model-agnostic (works with any model that can be queried for predictions), slightly less computationally efficient than tree SHAP, and produces different explanation artifacts (linear approximation weights rather than additive game-theoretic values).

items: Local approximation — fits simple model to local neighborhood.
Model-agnostic — works with any queryable model.
Linear explanation — feature weights from simple model.
Accurate locally — explains behavior near specific input.
Complementary — different artifact than SHAP values.

content.title: Why it matters
content.text: LIME works with any model and provides local explanations — making it widely applicable across model types and use cases.

sections.title: SHAP vs. LIME: Which to use
sections.description: Both have strengths — SHAP is more rigorous and efficient for tree models; LIME is more model-agnostic and widely applicable.

content.text: Both tools are widely used and each has practical strengths. SHAP produces more theoretically rigorous attributions and is particularly efficient for gradient-boosted tree models — the most common model type for enterprise tabular ML. LIME is more model-agnostic and can work with any black-box model through query-based perturbation. ClickMasters evaluates both for your specific model type and regulatory context, sometimes using both together since they can produce complementary explanations.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of AI explainability tools

content.text: AI explainability tools have limitations. SHAP and LIME can disagree on attribution values. Explanation quality depends on model complexity. SHAP approximations for neural networks may be less accurate. LIME explanations are only locally valid. Computational cost increases with feature count and model complexity. Explanations can be misused as definitive causal analysis. SHAP values are model-specific — retraining changes explanations. Human interpretation of SHAP outputs requires training.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about AI explainability tools

items.question: Do SHAP and LIME always agree on which features are most important?
items.answer: They often agree on the most important features but can differ on the precise attribution values, particularly for models where the decision boundary is highly nonlinear — ClickMasters investigates meaningful disagreements rather than treating one method as definitively correct.

items.question: Can SHAP explain why the model chose a specific probability, not just a binary prediction?
items.answer: Yes — SHAP explains the model's predicted probability (or regression value) in addition to any threshold-based binary decision.

items.question: How do we present SHAP explanations to non-technical stakeholders?
items.answer: ClickMasters builds human-readable explanation templates from SHAP outputs appropriate for your specific audience — regulatory reports, customer-facing explanations, or management summaries have different presentation requirements.

items.question: How long does integrating explainability tools take?
items.answer: 4–14 weeks depending on model complexity and reporting requirements.

items.question: Do SHAP explanations change if the model is retrained?
items.answer: Yes — SHAP explanations are model-specific; retraining the model produces new explanations that should be validated for consistency with expected feature behavior.

items.question: Can SHAP detect if a model is relying on proxy features for protected characteristics?
items.answer: SHAP can surface which features are most influential for specific predictions or population segments, contributing to bias audit — ClickMasters uses this alongside dedicated fairness testing rather than relying on SHAP alone for bias detection.

items.question: What is the difference between local and global explanations?
items.answer: Global explanations describe overall model behavior; local explanations describe why the model made a specific prediction for a specific input. SHAP and LIME are primarily local explanation tools.

items.question: Can SHAP and LIME be used for deep learning models?
items.answer: Yes — SHAP has DeepSHAP for neural networks; LIME is model-agnostic and works with any model. However, approximation quality varies with model complexity.

items.question: Are SHAP and LIME sufficient for regulatory compliance?
items.answer: SHAP and LIME can support regulatory explanation requirements but may not be sufficient alone — ClickMasters recommends legal counsel for compliance determinations and combines SHAP/LIME with other validation methods.
